topics.title: About this volume
topics.summary: A program becomes a product when someone other than its original author can build it, verify its behavior, diagnose a failure, and operate the delivered artifact. This volume follows HarborMetrics, a small measurement-processing application, from repository organization through release evidence. The examples are deliberately small enough to inspect, but their engineering questions are the same ones that appear in much larger systems.

blocks.text: The default examples use C++20 and the shared CMake build. Run performance experiments in an optimized build after correctness tests, record the machine and workload, and do not compare sanitizer timings with ordinary release timings.

topics.title: Learn from contracts, not isolated syntax
topics.summary: Read the numbered concepts first, then follow the worked example. Each chapter includes complete source files, an explanation of the mechanism, a practice task, and solution notes. The examples are teaching programs with explicit scope; they are not a promise of production certification. Run the supplied checks before modifying an example, then add a failing case that captures the behavior you intend to change.

topics.summary: The primary CPU source baseline is C++20. The CUDA translation units use a deliberate C++17 subset at their host/device boundary. CMake 3.24 or later, a compatible compiler and standard library, Python 3.10 or later, and a build tool are required. Installation guidance is in Book I; platform-specific procedures are explicitly labeled. No third-party download is required by the default CPU examples.

topics.title: Verification and portability boundaries
topics.summary: This edition includes the actual TEST_REPORT.md and build logs in the ZIP. CPU tests were run on the recorded Linux environment; those finite checks are not exhaustive proofs. The report distinguishes compiler runs, sanitizers, optional tooling, document checks, and unsupported environments.

blocks.text: No CUDA compiler or NVIDIA GPU was available in the publishing environment. CUDA source is provided with checked runtime calls, CPU references, and a target-machine validation procedure, but it has not been compiled or executed here. CPU success must never be reported as a GPU pass. Windows, macOS, multiple GPUs, hard-real-time scheduling, and hardware-specific performance are not validated by the Linux CPU tests. Observed timings in runnable examples are measurements of the reader’s run; hypothetical models are explicitly labeled.

topics.title: Use evidence to close the learning loop
topics.summary: Keep the input, expected result, observed result, compiler version, flags, and platform with each experiment. A correctness check and a benchmark answer different questions. A passing sanitizer run does not prove the absence of every defect; a faster timing does not excuse an invalid result. Chapter solutions explain the reasoning rather than merely giving an answer string.
